methods: setting up conditions for a common root
statement: The quadratics $x^{2}+px+q=0$ and $x^{2}+rx+s=0$ have a common root. Show that $(q-s)^{2}=(p-r)(ps-qr)$.
solution: Let the common root be $\alpha$. Then $\alpha^{2}+p\alpha+q=0$ and $\alpha^{2}+r\alpha+s=0$. Subtracting gives $(p-r)\alpha+(q-s)=0$, so (assuming $p\neq r$) $\alpha=\frac{s-q}{p-r}$. Substituting $\alpha$ back into the first equation and clearing denominators gives the required relation: $(q-s)^{2}=(p-r)(ps-qr)$.
hints: Let alpha be the common root.
Subtract the two equations to isolate alpha.
